questions.q: What is the universal security rule for dynamic SQL that applies on every platform in this comparison?
options: Only T-SQL requires bind variables; the other platforms are immune to SQL injection
Dynamic SQL should never be used under any circumstances
Bind variables are optional as long as the input is numeric
Always use bind variables/parameters for any dynamic SQL incorporating user input — never string-concatenate untrusted input into the SQL text
questions.explain: SQL injection is possible on every platform when untrusted input is concatenated directly into SQL text — bind variables/parameters prevent this everywhere, not just on one platform.

questions.q: What makes MySQL's dynamic SQL model structurally different from PL/SQL's and PL/pgSQL's?
options: MySQL cannot use bind variables for dynamic SQL
MySQL uses a distinct three-statement cycle: PREPARE, EXECUTE ... USING, and DEALLOCATE PREPARE, rather than one single statement
MySQL's dynamic SQL requires no placeholders of any kind
MySQL has no dynamic SQL capability at all
questions.explain: Unlike PL/SQL's single EXECUTE IMMEDIATE statement or PL/pgSQL's single EXECUTE statement, MySQL splits the process into three separate statements: PREPARE, EXECUTE, and DEALLOCATE PREPARE.

questions.q: What placeholder style does PL/SQL's EXECUTE IMMEDIATE use for bind variables?
options: Dollar-numbered placeholders like $1
Positional placeholders like ? only
Named placeholders like :id, filled by the USING clause
PL/SQL does not support placeholders in dynamic SQL
questions.explain: PL/SQL's EXECUTE IMMEDIATE uses named bind variables such as :id inside the SQL string, filled in by the USING clause.

questions.q: What is T-SQL's safer dynamic SQL path, as opposed to EXEC() which has no parameter support?
options: EXECUTE IMMEDIATE
PREPARE/EXECUTE
T-SQL has no safer alternative to EXEC()
sp_executesql, which supports parameters similarly to a stored procedure
questions.explain: sp_executesql accepts a parameter definition string and parameter values, letting you avoid concatenating user input directly into the SQL text, unlike the less safe EXEC().

questions.q: What placeholder style does PL/pgSQL's EXECUTE statement use?
options: Named placeholders like :id, identical to PL/SQL
PL/pgSQL does not support dynamic SQL
Question-mark placeholders like ?, identical to MySQL
Dollar-numbered positional placeholders like $1, filled by the USING clause
questions.explain: PL/pgSQL's EXECUTE 'sql' INTO var USING val; uses $1-style positional placeholders, distinct from PL/SQL's named :id style and MySQL's ? style.
